Unrailed is a simple, primarily multiplayer co-op mini-game. It is NOT an open world survival crafting game, it should not have that tag.

In Unrailed you have a train that is slowly moving right towards the edge of the screen while you and up to 3 friends, mine rocks and chop down trees to both make way and build more tracks. In the "endless" game mode you start in the first, easiest world and work your way up to the final hardest world, getting upgrades for your train along the way. In "quick" mode you pick a world and play a 15 minute round. There is also versus, sandbox and time, but these modes feel like an afterthought and most players will stick to the first two.

Unrailed is basically a party game. You boot it up with friends, play a few rounds or see how far you can get, laugh at the hi-jinks, and then move on to something else. Its not set up for a long campaign you return to multiple times or single player. So keep that in mind. While it does allow for saves and for you to pick up where you left off, its clear that is not really the intended way to play. It took my friends and I, a 2 to 3 hour run to beat the game, though we did that after several unsuccessful runs. If your goal is only to beat the game, and you don't look at a guide, expect to spend maybe 6 to 10 hours depending on whether you use checkpoints.

That said, it is very fun for what it is. The simple mechanics are easily picked up by anyone but the challenges it throws at you late game can be difficult. I played all the way through with 3 friends who are all avid gamers and we struggled at times. But on lower difficulties you can still give the game a try with kids or people who don't game much.

Lastly, I did enjoy the art style and the music. Seriously, the sound track is better than it has any right to be. Its all very polished and cute.

In the end, I would recommend this game on sale. $20 is a bit much considering you and all your friends need to pay that, and its not really worth buying for solo play. But for $10 or less I think its well worth it.

Unrailed! shows that a fun game doesn't require a big budget. Its simplistic game design makes it easy to understand for young and old, while the increasing challenge of the accelerating train keeps it interesting even for hardcore gamers. The game never gets boring because of its procedurally generated maps, which forces you to remain alert about where to build the track and mine resources. One small thing I enjoyed a lot was those exploding fish in the Underwater DLC. They grow in size and explode if you're close to them, but if you time it well, you can dash away and stay alive and basically get a free level 5 dynamite.
There are 4 difficulty levels that vary the amount of resources and bottlenecks. On Easy, it's easy to build the track straight to the right, while on Hard there are more resources and mountains in the way. The Extreme difficulty isn't very fun imo, as it just becomes Bottleneck Simulator. Interestingly, the difficulty levels don't vary the train speeds.
The co-op gives a whole new layer of variety as each online player has their own ideas and skill sets. I recommend to have people join early and not mid or late game because it takes a bit of time to build up the team spirit. Not to mention there is always that small but nonzero chance of getting a troll who destroys your track, which you wouldn't want in late game. I want to note that the multiplayer was programmed very well. You barely notice your high ping even when playing on Asian servers. The game also repairs itself well even when the connection goes bad. I feel like a lot of other games would've desynced and closed the game. You can always rejoin when you are kicked by bad connection.
The game is also surprisingly playable in single player. The bot is not always very smart (shuttling back and forth between two locations as a miner, in rare cases getting stuck behind a lake), and it gets in the way sometimes, but you can give it specific tasks and even set the location for them. I managed to do 2k meters on Easy with just the bot.
My only serious critique is the lack of in-game chat. This makes it impossible to discuss strategy, communicate if you're going for an achievement, or just to tell jokes or compliment your team. I would also simply like to chat with my Chinese comrades. Without in-game chat, the game feels dead.
Their defense may be that they have a Discord server, but I don't think it's sufficient. Not everyone uses Discord to play this game, nor does it work as in-game chat. Besides, Discord isn't really a thing in China.

For singleplayer:

Had to sleep but added him and I am pretty sure we will get to the 1k+. This all without voice chat, the in-game emotes were enough!
Don't want to meet up with randoms? The bot is there for you. 
Although maybe not for everyone; if you have a quick mind you can use it pretty effectively. Certainly a fun brain exercise :)

Unrailed is the definition of raw, unadulterated multiplayer fun. The constant ticking clock of the train moving forward creates a lot of tension and beautiful moments where you and your crew are fighting for your lives to get rail extended at the end of the line. The way that resources are managed - i.e. requiring you to cut down trees and rocks to create new rails while also creating space for new rail - is just incredible for such a simple game. Balancing your wood usage for rails and for bridging out to collectables or new areas is fun and engaging in a way that is difficult to describe. Fighting off the enemies with your pickaxe with friends is funny and creates opportunities for all sorts of hilarious moments. The fact that your character cannot walk through other characters or through terrain pieces or the train makes for an additional challenge that you not only need to make room for the train and its rails but also yourself and space to work around the rails. The game is challenging but fair and repetitive but engaging, a complete package for a simple indie-game. Don't bother picking it up if you can't con any friends into playing with you!

Look, I'm giving this a positive review, but there's a lot of caveats to this recommendation. If any of the below sounds like a no-go to you, then I'd suggest passing this game up. Also, keep in mind that while I have 20+ hours of this game on record, a lot of that is from showing it to different friends and letting them play while I watched. Chances are if you're going to play this with 1-3 friends, you're more likely going to get 5-10 hours of enjoyment out of this, which I think is pretty reasonable for the couch co-op genre.

Also, I think this without saying: while there is a "singleplayer" mode, definitely do not purchase this if you plan on playing alone. Like overcooked, this game thrives on being played with 2-4 players.

First of all, the overall aesthetic is fantastic. Each area looks fabulous, and the selection of music is really great (especially the desert-themed tracks). I love the attention to detail here: each area takes the same gameplay concepts and changes their visual appearance completely to keep things fresh. Even the music makes some interesting transitions alongside the weather/environment: the same song might sound different depending on if it's raining, foggy, or nighttime.

Most importantly, the core gameplay loop has tapped into something really special, something I haven't experienced in other couch co-op games. Think of it as a combination of overcooked's resource management and some light minecraft elements. You tear down forests and rocks to produce rails to keep the train moving through procedurally generated environments. As you complete levels and collect "bolts," you upgrade your train with new carts that can automine, produce TNT, create light, and more. Eventually, your train becomes too fast to manage, and you move on to a new biome, six in total.

All of this works really well and creates some really organic, tense gameplay. Situations can get really crowded, so you always need to think ahead on how much space/resources you have to continue to move forward. Of the 10-15 people I have played this game with, almost everyone fell in love with it. What really works here is the sense of adventure. Each biome has some great gameplay changes that keep things interesting, and what drove my friends and I forward was the desire to see what each new level had in store. I think the three difficulties create their own neat variety as well, with easy mode giving you a lot of space to work, and hard mode having dense forests you have to cut through.

So, the game's great. What are the caveats?

For starters, a lot of the core gameplay feels unbalanced. While there is a lot of variety when it comes to the train car upgrades, there really isn't any incentive to using anything other than the ghost train, the tnt maker, and the autominer. All of the other train cars have fun gimmicks to them, but lack any longterm benefits. Take the torch train, for example. Sure having additional light during nighttime segments is nice in theory, but when night only occurs every five minutes of gameplay or so and the final area doesn't have a day/night cycle, there's never a point where you'd want this car. It's especially useless because you can't remove the cart after you purchase it, making it dead weight that just crowds your already really long train. So, while it looks like there's a lot of unique variety, you'll find yourself avoiding most upgrades because they are simply useless. Just look at the world record runs for this game-- they all exclusively use the TNT car and nothing else.

Perhaps what's most damning about this game is it's length. Depending on how many people you play with, the speed of your train will change to balance out how many extra hands you have. If you have four players, the train speeds up pretty quickly. With two players, however, the train slows down to make up for the fact that you both are balancing multiple jobs at once. That being said, two player games can take a [i]really[/i] long time because you're covering the same amount of ground as a four player game but everything takes longer. Getting to the sixth and final biome could take several hours of a playthrough depending on how much time you spend upgrading your train, even with four people.

As a pick-up-and-play couch co-op game, this can be really frustrating. Often times when I showed this to friends, we would spend thirty minutes in the starting biome and run out of time before things got exciting because progression is way too slow. It's almost as if this game is stuck between wanting to be an adventure game and pick-up-and-play high score game. I personally found more fun with the game when I treated it like an adventure game, using save files (which negates high scores) to see where the next biome would take us. Luckily, I had friends who were willing to invest a few days on the same playthrough instead of getting bored with the game. I can't imagine what it would be like to play this game in one sitting. Just look at the "world record" runs on Youtube-- some of them are 7+ hours long. That sounds awful.

The last thing I want to mention is the Dev team's work in early access. Early on updates were great; a sixth biome was added alongside save files and a handful of other cool things. Then, around December 2019 it was radio silence on updates. Every once in a while they would throw in a few new player skins and the (half baked) single player update, but the rest of the year was spent on community challenge posts that died out pretty quickly as well. I understand that Covid-19 has probably thrown a wrench in their initial development plans, but with the game planning on going to 1.0 this month with zero meaningful updates this year, I'm hesitant that we're going to see many of these issues improved. I'm especially uneasy about the $5 price bump and the zero information we have on what 1.0 is going to include.

What's frustrating about this is that the core gameplay is so tight I could easily see a full game based on these concepts being a lot of fun. Things like a challenge mode, a full-fledged singleplayer, or even some gameplay modifiers could do a lot to make this a full-fledged experience. But as of right now, there isn't much to do outside of the main survival mode: the both the 2v2 multiplayer mode and the singleplayer feel incredibly half-baked.

So, if any of the above seems like a red flag to you, I'd pass on this. If not, definitely pick it up, but maybe not for the full $20. That being said, I really enjoyed my time with this game, as the gameplay and sense of adventure is really something special for the couch co-op genre, so it's a thumbs up for me.

Fun game for those who are into co-op games, with a very broad range of difficulty. The game has quite a few things going for it. First off, a very simple control system that is easy to learn but not overly minimalist. Next, a cute artstyle that is light on performance. Also, it features a roguelite system of being able to upgrade your train (though more on this later). Lastly, the game oftentimes creates a crazed panic between you and your companions as you desperately try to keep the train going.

Overall, especially with friends, you will almost certainly have fun. However, I have a few problems with the game. My biggest problem is with how difficulty works. There are three ways the game incorporates difficulty: the setting you choose at the beginning of the game, which I'll refer to as the "difficulty setting" and the speed of the train, which increases as you progress, and biomes, which get progressively harder. The difficulty setting determines how hard the layout of the map is, not at all how the speed of the train increases/functions nor the difficulty of the biomes. Therefore, for me and my friends, who usually played on the Medium difficulty setting, the early few stages were quite a breeze. But, after a certain point, the difficulty just spikes and we find ourselves dying quickly. To me it feels odd that the terrain generation (i.e. the amount of resources and impassable rock) does NOT scale (unless you count specific biome hazards), while the other two aspects do. Something just feels off about the early game.

Other than that, this game is not really one you can go back to again and again and grind out in my opinion, as it lacks much content. Yes there are new wagons to buy and new characters to unlock, but imo there are not enough of either to make the game feel constantly fresh.

This game is a lot of fun. Although I may not have as many hours logged as I would like, this is a very very enjoyable game. There are a lot of different roles to play and as the game evolves, so does the play style of each team.

In a 4 player game you have:
1 person in charge of chopping wood
1 person in charge of mining ore
1 person in charge of laying track
1 person in charge of managing resources and keeping the engine cool. 

With less players, the defined roles merge into each other but the game is still a lot of fun to play. But I feel that the best part of the game is the option to add new wagon parts and upgrade them as you go along. You can find yourself playing one game with a bunch of dynamite charges or another game where you farm cattle for milk that gives you bonus power-ups. 

The game has a lot of replayability in terms of the train you build, the team you play with and the different biomes you get to see. I do think  that less than 3 players is a much less fun experience. If you cannot find the discord or do not want to play with people, this is not a game for you.

The fun of this game comes from the people you play with and the hilarious situations you get into as the game gets harder and harder. This is a perfect example of a couch co-op similar to Overcooked or Castle Crashers. You get more fun out of the game based on the people you get to play with. The game is just here to bring us together and force us to work together. 

I do hope the dev team improves the game even more as the dev team gets out of early access. I am partially colorblind and some of the colors mesh for me and make it hard to pick out distances or location on the map. 
I wish characters were more pronounced on screen, as well as dropped items like the pickaxe, axe, bucket. The game relies on you having access to speak directly with team members via mic over the internet or in the same room with you. Without a mic you can only communicate with an emotes wheel that has the fundamental symbols of the game (ie wood, iron, axe, pickaxe, thumbs up, thumbs down) or using the Q key to highlight things on the map. This is a nice touch but so basic that its almost useless as the game is all about efficiency and min maxing your movement+actions. So do be aware that communication is VERY important, and if you can't talk to your team it will be harder to play. 

I know this is a longer review, but I hope it helps people who are on the fence. I enjoy the game and I also was lucky enough to find the Discord channel which has made my experience MUCH MUCH better. Without the Discord I would probably have refunded the game since finding people is impossible without the Discord and the "matchmaking" doesn't seem to work with pairing random people together. Each time I play I learn something new and get a good laugh out of the game. If you are looking for a really fun and entertaining co-op game, I can highly recommend this as a great option.

Unrailed!—the game where you and your friends build a train track in real-time, racing against the clock to keep the train from derailing into the abyss. Sounds relaxing, right? WRONG. It’s like a stressful train-themed nightmare, but somehow, it’s also ridiculously fun.

If you like trains, this game is for you. If you don’t like trains, well... you’re about to develop a love-hate relationship with them. You and your crew will be frantically chopping trees, mining rocks, and laying tracks, all while the train just keeps chugging along, ready to crash into whatever obstacle you didn’t clear in time. And let me tell you, the panic sets in fast.

The game quickly turns into a chaotic mess of shouting things like, "WE NEED MORE TRACKS!" and "WHO SET THE FOREST ON FIRE?!" (pro tip: keep an eye on your train’s water supply, or you’ll find yourself in a fiery disaster). It’s a game where teamwork is essential, but if one of your friends decides to go rogue or get distracted by something shiny, the whole operation falls apart faster than a Jenga tower.

Stressful? Absolutely. But also addictive and full of meme-worthy moments like accidentally running over your own track and screaming "TRAIN!!!" at the top of your lungs.

Randy Rating: 4.4/5 — Love trains? You’ll love this. Hate stress? Too bad—you’ll be building tracks like your life depends on it.

Unrailed is a unique multiplayer adventure where collaboration is essential. Build tracks in procedural worlds, upgrade your train and avoid derailments with your friends.

I always come back to Unrailed on a random day at 2 or 3 am. It has a very simple game loop: Break stuff, carry materials, build tracks, place tracks, and try to not make a bad choice while doing any of that. This loop makes my brain turn off as I automatically follow the simple instructions, and it can be a bit addictive at times. I love when I play with strangers too, despite there not being much communication. It's just Me and three strangers, chilling at 3 am, building tracks to move forward in a silly train game. I decided to write this because I love the amount of support the game was given. The game had been given tons of support until the sequel was released. Even after the sequel, both games are very distinct gameplay-wise, and there is very good reason to play both. Personally, I appreciate the complexity that is introduced throughout the first game as it increases in difficulty.

As a father of a 4 year old this is a brilliant same screen co-op cosy game about building railways. Teaches team-work, focus under pressure, problem solving and route planning. The biggest problem is more-or-less inherent in games designed to start from the beginning: The mechanics added/changed in later levels ("biomes") are easy enough to figure out if you can experiment; however, simply getting far enough to experiment with them is a large time commitment. The game has optional checkpoints, but mostly implies that said checkpoints aren't intended for part of a "proper" play. If you follow that implication, the difficulty curve will suddenly sharpen when you get to the snow or lava biomes, as you won't make far enough to see them often enough to figure out the tricks for navigating them. Of course, fixing this sort of problem takes clever creativity (or getting the players to swallow their pride, which is probably harder).

In addition, I personally dislike some of the mechanics in the 3rd & 4th biomes: Slowed movement, restricted visibility, and rotated camera. There's also mechanics for working around the slowed movement, so it's not as frustrating as it sounds, although they're mostly unintuitive and require experimenting to discover (see preceding paragraph). Positives: The voxel art of this game is great. The basic gameplay is easy to learn. The game is well-balanced and interesting enough to keep you going. It generates maps from random seeds, which gives you a potentially unlimited amount of slightly different maps to play.

Negatives: There are some major flaws.
[olist]
[*] There is no cloud save. Any unlock items are local and disappear when you switch machine.
[*] There is no career mode that allows you to progressively get familiar with all the elements of the game. Instead, one has to play in endless mode to get a “playthrough” of the game.
[*] There isn't any well-designed tutorial. You can indeed learn the most basic control from the current tutorial, but that is all. You may spend a large amount of time on trial and error in endless mode to learn how to deal with other biomes; how to use other wagons; when to choose which upgrade; how to deal with animals and bandits; etc. For example, how am I supposed to know it is mandatory to collect all orange bolts in order to get to the terminal, when I am new to this game? The lack of a proper tutorial is even more frustrating due to the flaw of the current save system mentioned below. If I omit to collect one orange bolt before getting to the next biome, I can no longer get to the terminal unless I restart the whole game! What a severe punishment for the ignorance of beginners.
[*] Last but the most important one, the save system is intendedly flawed. Currently, one is only allowed to save at each checkpoint in Kids difficulty. In any other difficulties, one can only save at the first checkpoint in a new biome. This save system, which is not clearly explained in the game itself hence causes many confusions, has several implications:
[list]
[*] The game is completely unfriendly towards beginners. Imagine that a beginner plays on Easy difficulty. When they get to a first-met and difficult biome, such as the space biome, it is understandable that they fail to get to the first station in this biome. In that case, BOOM, they are sent back to the [b]FIRST[/b] station in the [b]LAST[/b] biome, a whole hour of time for nothing!
[*] A non-beginner cannot enjoy playing on a higher difficulty without sacrificing the ability to save at each checkpoint.
[/list]
[/olist]

This flawed save system is the major deal-breaker for me. It has been a quite frustrating experience to get to the terminal for the first time. All these problems can be easily fixed by introducing a checkbox allowing players to save at each checkpoint in higher difficulty, and change the save in each biome to be the last station in that biome. In that way, the game is much more friendly to players of any level. This save issue is mentioned by countless players in the reviews or posts in the forum. However, the developers refuse to make such a simple change, with the excuse that the scores on difficulties other than Kids will be submitted to the leaderboard hence adding more checkpoints is not fair. But hey, you could just disable the score submission whenever the player chooses to save at each checkpoint! How hard is it to figure this out?

As a casual player who has no intention to compete for the leaderboards, I am quite disappointed by the developers' attitude towards the problems I have mentioned above. So for now, I do not recommend this game to other casual players. Will definitely change if these issues are fixed.

As far as co-op party games go, I would classify Unrailed as Excellent.

The premise is fairly straightforward: a train that cannot stop needs a railroad built ahead of it before it derails and crashes. The task for you and your co-op friends, is to collect wood and stone to craft rails so you can lay track ahead of the train to prevent it from derailing. If the train reaches the end of the track before you lay your next piece, you lose. If you successfully navigate the procedurally generated level to the end and your train makes it safely to the next train station, you progress to the next level.

The big challenge is working cooperatively with your team. Every piece of rail requires 1 wood and 1 stone. But there is only 1 axe for chopping wood and one pickaxe for breaking stone per level. So you have to be very intentional and efficient with who is doing what task. We often assigned woodcutter, stonecutter, track maker, and track layer roles. This helped keep jobs defined and assigned, and helped us stay out of each other's way (there is player collision so you have to be careful in tight chasms!)

The levels also get more difficult as you progress. In the early game, you are mostly concerned with cutting paths through forests and mountains. But as the game goes on, certain areas cannot be destroyed, so you have to be careful which direction you choose to take your train. Even further into the game, the environments start to change, adding new upgrades for your train, but also new challenging terrain to navigate.

I like the train modules. I like how you have to input wood and stone so it produces a rail. I like how you can upgrade your existing modules, and add new modules, between levels. The pacing of the game was very good. The end game levels are very challenging, but by the time you get to them, the difficulty has increased at a reasonable, incremental level, so you feel adequately prepared for the challenge. The different difficulty settings make it easy to turn up the heat when you want a more difficult, chaotic experience. I also liked that the game challenges you to find rare currency on each level to use to upgrade your train, which gives you incentive to explore and pay attention, and it gives a secondary objective besides simply surviving to the end of the level.

In my experience, the multiplayer connectivity was excellent. We never had any issues with the netcode.

I would highly recommend this game for anyone looking for an engaging co-op puzzle/party game. To compare it to other similar games, I would say it reminds me of the co-op chaos of the Overcooked series, Out of Space, and Lovers in a Strange Spacetime.

[b]More about the game[/b]

You have something to do all the time even with two other players. I tend to take the role of leader while wife and daughter gather materials. Daughter tends to go for woodcutting (not bringing it to train) and helps with water, wife does iron and delivers it to the train. I'm going for water, collecting resources, build bridges, sets general direction where we are going and where the girls should go for materials. I also lay down track. Sometimes I have hard times managing all that. But girls are getting better and better so I don't have so much to think about :-)

Once the train goes it never stops, there is constant stress put on the players and it fuels the game. It can be played in 5-10 minutes increments and saved in the meantime while you are at a station. You can also buy upgrades there for faster making of tracks or bigger storage for input materials. You can build new wagons that add some functionality to your train (compass to show the way, dynamite maker to clean the way, "exchanger" to make iron from wood and vice versa, light to lighten up the night, ...).

I can imagine the game is fun even when playing "internet" multiplayer. But really - it is best when all the players are on the same couch in front of one TV.

Recommended ONLY IF you have friends to play it with, and even then, maybe only if you're running out of good games to play. This was whopping fun for a few runs, and then our group ran into two major problems:

1) Dying means having to replay the previous instead of current biome, which means losing a ton of progress, AND not being able to follow up on our mistakes and practise immediately (one of THE worst problems in games). Maybe this is to help prevent being locked into bad builds or something, but that should be a comparatively minor issue?

2) The biomes are all super easy until the hell biome which is super hard, mainly due to a few new mechanics being thrown at us with little explanation and time to figure things out before the train crashes. Coupled with the first problem, this became a huge momentum killer for our group.

Relaxing? Nah. But it’s not brutal either—just chaotic enough. Me and my clumsy crew stuck to easy, and we still fumbled.
Clean pixel art, no complaints there. Only buzzkill? That one-time save. Killed our mood fast.
No stopping the train—just lay track. If the save thing doesn’t bug you, it’s worth it.
